Araunah
uh-RAW-nuh
proper noun (Old Testament figure)
Araunah (Hebrew Aravnah; called Ornan in Chronicles) was a Jebusite of Jerusalem; the name is of Jebusite origin, possibly meaning "lord" or "noble."

📖 Biblical Definition

Araunah the Jebusite, named Ornan in the Chronicles, owned the threshingfloor upon Mount Moriah where the plague that followed David's sinful numbering of the people was stayed. When the angel of the LORD stood between earth and heaven with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, the prophet Gad commanded David to rear an altar in the threshingfloor of Araunah. The Jebusite, seeing the king come, would have freely given the floor, the oxen for sacrifice, and the threshing instruments for wood; but David refused, saying, Nay, but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the place and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, and reared an altar, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the LORD answered him and stayed the plague. This narrative is a true history of mercy after judgment, and it carries a great typology: the site of Araunah's floor became the very place where Solomon built the temple, the house of sacrifice for all Israel, and so the appointed place of atoning blood. David's confession—that worship which costs nothing is no worship—abides as a standing rebuke to cheap and careless religion, and the bought threshingfloor points forward to the costly sacrifice of Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Jebusite whose threshingfloor David bought for an altar, the site of the staying of the plague and of the future temple.

ARAUNAH, proper noun. A Jebusite of Jerusalem, called Ornan in Chronicles; owner of the threshingfloor on Moriah.

The man from whom David purchased the place to build an altar to the LORD.

His threshingfloor became the site of Solomon's temple.

As it is written, "neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing" (2 Sam 24:24).

A type of the costly sacrifice required by God and fulfilled in Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

2Sa 24:18 — "And Gad came that day to David, and said unto him, Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite."

2Sa 24:24 — "And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver."

1Ch 21:25 — "So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight."

1Ch 22:1 — "Then David said, This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Araunah faces no postmodern redefinition, but David's principle of costly worship is widely forgotten in an age of convenient religion.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is that true worship costs the worshipper something. David refused to offer to the LORD that which cost him nothing, buying the threshingfloor and the oxen rather than accepting them as a gift. Cheap, careless, and convenient religion, which gives God the leftovers of time and treasure, stands rebuked by this Jebusite's floor.

The deeper lesson is the typology of the place itself. The threshingfloor where the plague was stayed became Mount Moriah, the site of the temple and its altar of burnt offering, the appointed place where atoning blood was shed for Israel. All of it pointed forward to the costly and once-for-all sacrifice of the Lord Jesus, who purchased His people not with silver and gold but with His own precious blood.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The account is rooted in David's sin of numbering Israel and in the mercy that appointed a place of sacrifice.

expand to see more

David's census of Israel brought a pestilence upon the land (2 Sam 24:15).

The angel of the LORD halted at the threshingfloor of Araunah (1 Chr 21:15).

Gad commanded David to build an altar in that place (2 Sam 24:18).

David bought the floor and oxen, refusing a free gift (2 Sam 24:24).

The site became Mount Moriah, where Solomon reared the temple (2 Chr 3:1).
